sheet.howExamined: M7, Paper 1 (no calculator) and Paper 2 (calculator), 50 marks in 75 minutes each. Counting appears about once a series, almost always on Paper 2 and in the second half of the paper, worth 3 marks. Two shapes recur. The two-part shape gives 1 mark for the plain product and 2 for a follow-on part that rules something out (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14; Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q7). The single-part shape lists three groups and asks for two of them, so three products are added for 3 marks (November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q16). The command words are "In how many ways" and "How many different"; a bare answer with no multiplication shown is vulnerable when the total is wrong.
traps: Adding the numbers of choices instead of multiplying them (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14; November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q16)
Leaving the repeated combinations in when the question asks for two different items (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14; Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q7)
Multiplying every group listed when only some of them are chosen (November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q16)
Counting only some of the pairs that can be made from three groups (November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q16)
Counting each pair twice, as if the two orders were different choices (November 2024 M7 Paper 2 Q16; Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14)
Starting a fresh multiplication for the second part instead of adjusting the total already found (Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14)
Keeping the full count at the second stage when the first choice cannot be used again (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q7)
Writing the total with no multiplication shown, so nothing is left to credit when the total is wrong (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q6; November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q5)

noteBlocks.caption: Every box is one breakfast deal: 4 rows of 3, so 4 $\times$ 3 $=$ 12 deals.

noteBlocks.prompt: On the breakfast table above, how many boxes are there in one row?
noteBlocks.explain: One row is one bread meeting each filling in turn, and there are 3 fillings.

noteBlocks.md:
The table is a rectangle, so the number of boxes is rows $\times$ columns. That is the whole rule.

**If one task can be done in $m$ ways, and for each of those the next task can be done in $n$ ways, the two together can be done in $m \times n$ ways.**

It is a multiplication because each of the $m$ first choices opens a fresh set of $n$ second choices, and none of those sets overlaps. Adding would give 7 here, which is fewer deals than the table plainly shows.

noteBlocks.prompt: A shop sells 5 shirt colours and 3 collar styles. How many different shirts can be ordered?
noteBlocks.explain: 5 $\times$ 3 $=$ 15. Each colour can have any of the 3 collars.

noteBlocks.md: Nothing changes when a third choice is added: you multiply again. A smoothie bar lets you pick one fruit from 5, one base from 4 and one of 2 sizes.

noteBlocks.md:
Write one box per stage, put the number of choices in each, then multiply across: 5 $\times$ 4 $\times$ 2 $=$ 40.

The boxes matter more than they look. They stop you multiplying a stage the question never asked for, and they stop you dropping one: 5 $\times$ 4 $=$ 20 would be the answer if size were fixed.

noteBlocks.why: Corbettmaths video 383 builds the rule from a short list and then stops listing, which is exactly the moment the multiplication earns its place. Watch it once, then answer the check below.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two choices are made, one after the other. What do you do with the numbers of ways?
noteBlocks.explain: Each way of making the first choice opens a whole fresh set of second choices, so the sets stack up by multiplication.

noteBlocks.text: When some combinations are ruled out

noteBlocks.md:
Exam questions often follow the count with a part that takes something back out. A parlour has 7 ice-cream flavours and 6 sorbet flavours, and 2 flavour names appear in both lists.

One scoop of each: 7 $\times$ 6 $=$ 42.

noteBlocks.prompt: Among those 42 ice-cream-and-sorbet pairs, how many use the same flavour twice?
noteBlocks.explain: Only the 2 names that appear in both lists can be paired with themselves, so 2 pairs repeat a flavour.

noteBlocks.md:
Two **different** flavours, then: the 2 repeated pairs come off, so 42 $-$ 2 $=$ 40.

Count everything first, then subtract. Trying to dodge the repeats while you multiply is what turns a two-line answer into a muddle.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q14
noteBlocks.md: Two lists of flavours, one scoop from each. Most candidates reached the product for the first part. The second part asked for two different flavours, and **only a minority took the repeats off the total** — the rest gave the full product or started a fresh multiplication.

noteBlocks.prompt: A deli offers 5 fillings and 5 salads. 3 names appear in both lists. How many filling-and-salad pairs use two different names?
noteBlocks.explain: 5 $\times$ 5 $=$ 25 pairs in all, then take off the 3 that repeat a name: 22.

noteBlocks.text: When a choice cannot be repeated

noteBlocks.md: A club of 12 picks a chairperson and then a secretary, and one person cannot hold both jobs.

noteBlocks.alt: Two boxes joined by a multiplication sign: Chairperson 12, Secretary 11.

noteBlocks.caption: The second box is 11, not 12: the chairperson is no longer available.

noteBlocks.md:
The first box is 12. The second is 11: whoever takes the first job is out of the running. So 12 $\times$ 11 $=$ 132 ways.

The jobs differ, so Ana as chair with Ben as secretary is a different outcome from Ben as chair with Ana. Both are counted.

noteBlocks.title: Why the second number drops
noteBlocks.md: The rule counts, for each first choice, the second choices still open. Once Ana is chair, 11 people remain, and that holds whoever is picked first. The number of second choices is the same every time, which is what lets you multiply.

noteBlocks.prompt: A squad of 14 picks a captain and then a different vice-captain. How many ways are there?
noteBlocks.explain: 14 $\times$ 13 $=$ 182. The captain cannot also be vice-captain, so the second number is 13.

noteBlocks.md:
Multiply the number of choices at each stage to count the outcomes.
Draw one box per stage so no stage is dropped or added.
Subtract the combinations a question rules out, after counting them all.
Drop the second number by one when the first choice cannot be repeated.

Usually one question in the second half of the paper, three marks, in two parts. The first mark is the product itself, written down: show the multiplication, not just the total. The last mark is the adjustment the second part asks for, taken off that total. Stuck: write the number of choices at each stage in a row and multiply across.

workedExamples.stem:
A hire shop beside the towpath rents out bikes.

There are 6 frame sizes and 4 helmet colours.

(a) In how many ways can a customer choose one frame size and one helmet colour?

(b) The shop adds 3 types of basket. Every customer now chooses a frame size, a helmet colour and a basket. In how many ways can that be done?

steps.working: Stage 1: frame size, 6 ways. Stage 2: helmet colour, 4 ways.
steps.decision: Name the stages before touching the numbers. A stage is one decision the customer makes, and the count beside it is how many ways that single decision can go.
Every frame size can be paired with every helmet colour, so the pairs fill a 6 by 4 rectangle. Adding would give 10, which is fewer than the frames alone can produce.

options: Because each frame size opens all the helmet colours again
Because there are more frames than helmets
Because the two numbers are close together
whyMenu.explain: For each of the 6 frames there are 4 helmets still to choose from, and those sets never overlap, so the total is 6 lots of 4.

steps.decision: A third decision is a third box. The rule does not change shape when a stage is added; it only gains a factor.
Carry the 24 from part (a) and multiply by 3, or multiply all three at once. Writing the multiplication out is what earns the method mark when the arithmetic slips.

twin.stem: A second shop has 5 frame sizes and 7 bell designs. In how many ways can a customer choose one frame size and one bell design?

items.stem: A two-way table has 5 rows and 3 columns. How many boxes are inside it?
items.skill: Read a two-way table as rows times columns

options.feedback: 5 rows of 3 boxes is 5 $\times$ 3 $=$ 15.
That is 5 $+$ 3. Adding counts one row and one column, not the whole rectangle.
That is the right count doubled. Each box is one place in the table and is counted once.
That is the number of rows. Every row holds several boxes.

items.stem: Nuala writes out every code made from one of the letters P and Q followed by one of the numbers 1, 2 and 3. How many codes does she write?
items.skill: List every pairing of two short lists systematically

options.feedback: P and Q each take three numbers, so the list is P1, P2, P3, Q1, Q2, Q3: 6 codes.
That is 2 $+$ 3, which counts the letters and numbers rather than the codes made from them.
That counts each code twice. The letter always comes first, so P1 and 1P are not two different codes.
That is the number of numbers. Each of them can follow either letter.

items.stem: A block of cubes is 2 cubes deep, 5 cubes wide and 4 cubes tall. How many cubes are in the block?

options.feedback: 2 $\times$ 5 $\times$ 4 $=$ 40.
That is 2 $\times$ 5, which is one layer. There are 4 layers.
Adding the three measurements does not count anything in the block.
That is 5 $\times$ 4, one slice of the block rather than all 2 of them.

items.stem: A van sells 6 kinds of wrap, 5 fillings and 4 drinks. How many different wrap-and-filling choices are there?
items.skill: Apply the product rule to exactly the stages the question names

options.feedback: 6 $\times$ 5 $=$ 30. The drinks are not part of this choice.
That is 6 $+$ 5. Each wrap can take any of the 5 fillings, so the choices multiply.
That multiplies the drinks in as well. The question asks for a wrap and a filling only, so the drinks box is not in this product.
That counts every choice twice. One wrap with one filling is a single choice however you write it down.

items.stem: A smoothie is made from one of 5 fruits, one of 4 bases and one of 2 sizes. How many different smoothies are there?

options.feedback: 5 $\times$ 4 $\times$ 2 $=$ 40.
That leaves the size out. Three decisions means three factors, so multiply by 2 as well.
Adding the three counts gives a number smaller than the fruits and bases alone can produce.
That is the right count doubled. Each smoothie is one fruit with one base in one size, counted once.

items.stem: A parlour has 7 ice-cream flavours and 6 sorbet flavours. 2 flavour names appear in both lists. How many ways are there to choose one scoop of each with two different flavours?
items.skill: Take the excluded combinations off the total

options.feedback: 7 $\times$ 6 $=$ 42, then take off the 2 pairs that repeat a flavour: 40.
That is every pair, including the 2 that use the same flavour twice. The question asks for two different flavours.
Only one repeated pair has been taken off. There are 2 flavour names in both lists, so 2 pairs come off.
Adding the two list lengths does not count pairs at all.

items.stem: A club of 12 members picks a chairperson and then a secretary. One person cannot hold both jobs. In how many ways can the two jobs be filled?
items.skill: Drop the second count when the first choice cannot be repeated

options.feedback: 12 $\times$ 11 $=$ 132. Whoever takes the first job is out of the running for the second.
That keeps all 12 available for the second job, which would let one person hold both.
That halves the count, which would be right if the two jobs were the same. Chairperson and secretary are different jobs, so both orders count.
Adding the two counts gives neither the pairs nor the people.

context.setting: Ordering a shirt in a colour and a collar style

parts.stem:
A shop sells shirts in 5 colours, each with a choice of 3 collar styles.

Work out the number of different shirts the shop sells.
hints: Each colour can have any of the collar styles.
One factor for the colour, one for the collar.
parts.workedSolution: Each of the 5 colours can take any of the 3 collars, so the count is 5 $\times$ 3 $=$ 15.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 5 $+$ 3. Every colour opens all 3 collars again, so the two counts multiply.
That is the right count doubled. A colour with a collar is one shirt, whichever you decide first.

context.setting: Setting a phone up with a ringtone and a wallpaper

parts.stem:
A phone comes with 9 ringtones and 6 wallpapers.

Each phone is set up with one ringtone and one wallpaper.

How many different set-ups are possible?
hints: Every ringtone can go with every wallpaper.

commonErrors.feedback: That adds the two lists. Adding would mean each phone got a ringtone or a wallpaper, not one of each.
Dividing compares the two lists rather than pairing them. The product rule multiplies.

context.setting: A wristband built from a band, a pattern and a clasp

parts.stem:
A stall makes wristbands to order.

There are 3 band colours, 5 patterns and 4 clasps.

Every wristband has one band colour, one pattern and one clasp.

How many different wristbands can be made?
hints: Write the three counts in a row and multiply across.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 3 $\times$ 5, with the clasp left out. The multiplication of the first two stages earns the method mark, so write the third factor in and the answer mark follows.

context.setting: Naming a captain and a vice-captain from one squad

parts.stem:
A hockey squad has 14 players.

A captain is named first, then a different player is named vice-captain.

In how many ways can the two roles be filled?
hints: The captain cannot also be vice-captain.
Once the captain is named, how many players are left for the second role?
parts.workedSolution: There are 14 choices of captain. The captain cannot take the second role, so 13 players are left for vice-captain: 14 $\times$ 13 $=$ 182 ways.

commonErrors.feedback: That keeps all 14 players available for the second role, so one player could hold both. The second factor is 13.
Halving would be right if the two roles were the same job. They are different, so captain Ana with vice-captain Ben and the other way round are two outcomes.

context.setting: A three-symbol entry code for a locker

parts.stem:
A locker code is 3 symbols long.

Each symbol is one of 4 shapes, and a shape may be used more than once.

How many different codes are possible?
hints: There is one stage for each position in the code.
A shape may be repeated, so nothing is used up.
parts.workedSolution: Each of the 3 positions can hold any of the 4 shapes, and repeats are allowed, so no count drops: 4 $\times$ 4 $\times$ 4 $=$ 64 codes.

commonErrors.feedback: That takes one shape out of play at each position. This code allows repeats, so all 4 shapes stay available every time.
The three positions have been added. Each position opens the full set of shapes again, so they multiply.

context.setting: A set menu whose number of puddings is unknown

parts.stem:
A set menu offers 9 main courses and some puddings.

A meal is one main course and one pudding.

There are 63 different meals.

Work out the number of puddings on the menu.
hints: The number of meals is the mains multiplied by the puddings.
Undo the multiplication with a division.
parts.workedSolution: The product rule gives 9 $\times$ puddings $=$ 63, so the number of puddings is 63 $\div$ 9 $=$ 7.

commonErrors.feedback: That undoes an addition. The meals came from a multiplication, so divide: 63 $\div$ 9.
Multiplying goes the wrong way: 63 already counts the meals, so the puddings come from dividing it by 9.

context.setting: A craft-fair gift pack holding two items of different kinds

parts.stem:
A craft stall sells 4 kinds of candle, 7 kinds of soap and 3 kinds of card.

A gift pack holds two items, and they must be of different kinds.

In how many ways can a pack be made from one candle and one soap?
hints: Every candle can go with every soap.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 4 $+$ 7. Each candle opens all 7 soaps again, so the counts multiply.
The cards have been multiplied in too. This part pairs a candle with a soap only.

parts.stem: How many different gift packs can be made altogether?

scheme.for: two further products from 4 x 3 = 12 and 7 x 3 = 21

hints: There are three ways to pick two different kinds.
Count each pairing separately, then add the three totals.

findTheMistake.stem: Órla was asked: a bakery sells 6 kinds of loaf and 4 kinds of spread, and a lunch box holds one loaf and one spread. How many different lunch boxes are there? Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 names the two stages correctly. Line 2 adds them. Adding counts the loaves and the spreads as separate things, but a lunch box is one of each, and every loaf can meet every spread. That is 6 rows of 4, so the counts multiply.
findTheMistake.feedback: A quick check catches this every time: there are already 6 boxes using the first spread alone, so a total of 10 cannot be right. Naming the stages first, as line 1 does, is the habit worth keeping.

prompts.prompt: One task can be done in $m$ ways and, for each of those, a second task can be done in $n$ ways. How many ways are there to do both?
A choice has three stages instead of two. What changes?
prompts.answer: Nothing changes except the number of factors: multiply all three counts together.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for two items that must be different. What do you do to the count?
prompts.answer: Work out the full product first, then subtract the combinations in which the two are the same.

prompts.prompt: Two different jobs are filled from a club of 12. Why is the second count 11?
prompts.answer: Whoever takes the first job cannot be chosen again, so only 11 people are left for the second.

prompts.prompt: Why does a two-way listing table show that the rule is a multiplication?
prompts.answer: Each row is one first choice and each column is one second choice, so the pairs fill a rectangle of rows times columns.

findings.asked: Two lists of flavours, one scoop from each; then the same choice with the two flavours required to differ.
findings.wentWrong: Many reached the product for the first part, some by drawing the whole listing table. The addition of the two list lengths was a common answer, as was the product doubled. In the second part a minority took the repeats off the total; others started a fresh multiplication.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the product down, then subtracted only the pairs that used the same flavour twice.
findings.rule: Count everything first, then take off what the question rules out.

findings.asked: Three groups of dishes, with two of the three chosen for a meal.
findings.wentWrong: Multiplication was used by most, and a few added. Some multiplied all three group sizes together although only two courses were ordered, some added only two of the three pairings, and some doubled the total by counting each pairing both ways round.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Worked out each pairing as its own product and added the three of them.
findings.rule: Multiply within a pairing, add between pairings, and count every pairing the question allows.

findings.asked: A counting question in two parts, the second excluding the repeated combinations.
findings.wentWrong: Nearly everyone earned the two marks for the plain count. Just under half managed the mark for discounting the repetitions.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Counted how many combinations repeated an item and subtracted exactly that many.
findings.rule: The exclusion mark is a subtraction from the total, not a new calculation.

findings.asked: The difference between the numbers of lunch combinations available on two days.
findings.wentWrong: Very well answered across the entry.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Counted each day with its own product and then compared the two totals.
findings.rule: Write the multiplication down even when the answer is quick: it is what survives an arithmetic slip.

findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Used the product rule without listing.
findings.rule: Once the stages are named, the count is one multiplication.

insight.ruleToRemember: One box per stage, the number of choices inside it, multiply across; then subtract anything the question rules out, and drop a count by one when a choice cannot be repeated.
insight.aStarSignal: Treating a two-from-three question as three separate products added together, without being prompted to split it.
